items.definition: a tendency to think or act in a way that unfairly favours one idea, person, or outcome

examples.source: Even trained professionals are not immune to bias when they feel rushed.
examples.translation: Selbst geschulte Fachleute sind nicht immun gegen Verzerrungen, wenn sie unter Zeitdruck stehen.

examples.source: The study examined how bias shapes what people notice and what they ignore.
examples.translation: Die Studie untersuchte, wie Voreingenommenheit beeinflusst, was Menschen wahrnehmen und was sie ignorieren.

examples.source: Recognising your own bias is uncomfortable, which is one reason it matters so much.
examples.translation: Die eigene Voreingenommenheit zu erkennen ist unangenehm, und genau deshalb ist es so wichtig.

examples.translation: Sie bewältigte die Unsicherheit, indem sie kleine Routinen schuf, die sie kontrollieren konnte.

examples.source: How people cope with grief often depends as much on support as on personality.

pages.text: One reason psychology fascinates so many people is that it gives names to experiences we already half recognise. We know what it feels like to cope with uncertainty, to ruminate after an awkward conversation or to notice that a small remark can trigger a response far out of proportion to the moment itself. We also know, if we are honest, that bias shapes our judgments even when we believe we are being reasonable.

Good psychological thinking does not promise perfect control. Instead, it helps us understand the patterns into which we repeatedly fall. Someone under stress may jump to conclusions because uncertainty feels unbearable. Another person may struggle to regulate emotions and then later feel ashamed of how they reacted. In both cases, perception is narrowed by pressure. What looks obvious in hindsight was not obvious at the time. Under strain, a person can fall into a pattern before noticing how automatic it has become.

That is why self-awareness matters. It creates a small pause between feeling and action, a pause in which choices become possible even when our feelings remain ambivalent. The aim is not to stop being human, but to understand the conditions under which we become defensive, avoidant, generous or brave. Seen this way, psychology is less about labelling people than about helping them live with greater freedom.
